An open biopsy of the right SI joint was subsequently performed, which revealed several lesions in the SI joint. Histology revealed multiple foci of cartilage surrounded by a rim of lamellar bone, consistent with multiple enchondromas (Figures 4(a), 4(b), and 4(c)). At 2-year follow-up, the patient is pain-free and has been evaluated with MRI with no evidence of recurrence.

He reported swelling in his right proximal tibia and worsening discomfort during ambulation. On physical exam, he had a palpable enlargement of his proximal tibia and multiple healed scars over the distal tibia from prior external fixation pins. Further evaluation with imaging was indicated. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and radiographs demonstrated an aggressive tumor with multiple areas of extraosseous extension (Figure 1A and B).

Pediatric rheumatology online journal 2022. doi:10.1186/s12969-022-00720-8. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Radiological examination at first presentation. a Presence of hyperclear, transverse bands on the distal phalanges, characteristic aspect of transverse acro-osteolysis (white arrow). b Presence of transverse lysis of the phalanges (white arrow) and modification of the bone structure of the metatarsals, appearance of a “fracture callus” (grey arrow). The overall symmetrical condition is noteworthy. c Numerous ovoid lesions, with clear centre and hyperdense outline reminiscent of intraosseous chondromes (white arrows). There is no sign of malignancy. d Appearance of a small spur with bellowing of the cortex, probably corresponding to a cortical point fracture (white arrow) and presence of chondromes
in_text_mentions: The first radiological examination found transverse AO of all the distal phalanges in both fingers and toes (Fig. 1a and b) and confirmed scoliosis.

A number of enchondromas and cortical defects were also found, located on the metaphysical part of the fibula and tibia (Fig. 1c and d). Sclerosis was found in the left horizontal branch of the mandibula, with no malignancy.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Radiograph of a pediatric patient with genetically confirmed genochondromatosis type 2 (IDH-1 mutation) showing longitudinal cartilage columns in metaphyseal regions, consistent with Ollier disease columnar pattern. [raw subtype: multiple enchondromatosis with columnar pattern] B: Radiograph of the same patient showing longitudinal cartilage columns in the metaphyseal regions of the tibias/fibulas, consistent with the multiple enchondromatosis columnar pattern of Ollier disease. [raw subtype: multiple enchondromatosis with columnar pattern] C: Radiograph of the same patient showing longitudinal cartilage columns in the metaphyseal regions of the distal radius/ulna and hand, consistent with the multiple enchondromatosis columnar pattern of Ollier disease. [raw subtype: multiple enchondromatosis with columnar pattern]
panels.attribution_text: Salduz et al. Rare radiological manifestation of enchondromatosis in children: Columnar pattern: A retrospective cohort study.. Medicine 2024. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000039106. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 14.
panels.figure_caption: Patient number 9, a 4-yr-old male, underwent genetic evaluation and was diagnosed with genochondromatosis type 2 with an IDH-1 mutation. Radiological evaluation revealed multiple affected physes bilaterally in all 4 extremities. It is a sporadic case with no family history. A longitudinal cartilage column was observed in each metaphyseal area. X-rays obtained at the last control at the age of 11 yr old revealed that the physes were still open (A,B,C). This patient is considered to be in the group of “multiple enchondromatosis with columnar pattern.”
in_text_mentions: Five patients had only one affected physis. Eight patients had 3 or less affected physis. The radiological features of the lesions which we defined as “limited enchondromatosis with columnar pattern” were shown in between Figures 2 and 13 (Figs. 2–13). The remaining 7 patients have multiple columns in multiple physis we defined these patient groups as “multiple enchondromatosis with columnar pattern.” Radiological appearances of the 3 out of 7 are shown in Figures 14 to 16 (patient number 9,10,11). These cartilage tissues were partially ossified during the follow-up.
